title.en: Water boils lower at altitude: the same trace at sea level and at 1,500 m

goal.en: Water and steam bands shift by minus 1 degC per 300 m. A reading of 97 degC is not a boil at sea level and is one in a mountain kitchen; a reading of 100 degC at 1,500 m is something a sensor should not see.

note.en: A pot that holds at 97 degC at sea level never reaches the 98 to 102 band.
The same readings at 1,500 m: the band is 93 to 97, and the pot is boiling.
A reading of 100 degC at 1,500 m is above the shifted band: water cannot be that hot there, so the sensor or the medium is in question.
At 2,400 m with a recipe target of 94 plus or minus 1: the target is checked inside the shifted band.

cli: printf '[{"t": 0, "tempC": 80}, {"t": 30, "tempC": 97}, {"t": 60, "tempC": 97}]' > trace.json && cookwala envelope cw.op.boil trace.json
printf '[{"t": 0, "tempC": 80}, {"t": 30, "tempC": 97}, {"t": 60, "tempC": 97}]' > trace.json && cookwala envelope cw.op.boil trace.json --altitude 1500
printf '[{"t": 0, "tempC": 80}, {"t": 30, "tempC": 100}, {"t": 60, "tempC": 100}]' > trace.json && cookwala envelope cw.op.boil trace.json --altitude 1500

outcome.en: You can validate boiling and simmering traces from kitchens at any altitude, and you have a test for sensors that read what physics forbids. Next: scenario 022 checks hot oil.
